classification.difficultyReason: Reconcile two apparently different primitives using logarithm laws and explain why the difference does not affect a definite integral.

content.prompt:
Stella found the primitive of the function $\frac{1}{5x}$ by taking out a factor of $\frac{1}{5}$,
$$\int\frac{1}{5x}\,dx=\frac{1}{5}\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx=\frac{1}{5}\ln|x|+C_1.$$
Bella used the standard form directly:
$$\int\frac{1}{5x}\,dx=\frac{1}{5}\ln|5x|+C_2.$$
Explain what is going on. Will this affect their result when finding a definite integral?

answer.short: Both methods are correct because $\ln|5x|=\ln5+\ln|x|$. Their constants satisfy $C_2=C_1-\frac{1}{5}\ln5$. For a definite integral, this constant difference cancels in $F(b)-F(a)$, so both methods give the same result.
answer.worked:
Using the logarithm law,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{5}\ln|5x|+C_2&=\frac{1}{5}\bigl(\ln5+\ln|x|\bigr)+C_2\\&=\frac{1}{5}\ln|x|+\frac{1}{5}\ln5+C_2.\end{align*}$$
Thus both methods describe the same family of primitives, with $C_1=\frac{1}{5}\ln5+C_2$, or $C_2=C_1-\frac{1}{5}\ln5$.
For a definite integral on an interval where the function is defined, the constant cancels when calculating $F(b)-F(a)$. Therefore both methods give the same result.
